pr_title: OSSL_PARAMS: Fix OSSL_PARAM_set_double() to not use ossl_[u]intmax_t
pr_body:
ossl_intmax_t and ossl_uintmax_t seem promissing.  Unfortunately, on
systems where they aren't standard typedefs, we typedef them as
aliases for long and unsigned long.

OSSL_PARAM_set_double() used this type for a very basic check of the
input value, with the assumption that these types would be large
enough to cover int64_t and uint64_t integers.  This turns out to be
a falacy, which causes failures of the test program
test/params_conversion_test.c.

The solution is to refactor the code so it doesn't use ossl_intmax_t
or ossl_uintmax_t for these type of checks.

Fixes #15815
pr_comments:
I think the problem lies with our definitions of intmax_t and uintmax_t not with the code here.  Instead of typedefing them as long, perhaps it should be long long or int64_t.

An alternative would be to use [u]int64_t instead of [u]intmax_t since that's the largest size we care about converting to/from.

issue_context.title: OSSL_PARAM_set_double() may fail on systems that do not define intmax_t
issue_context.body:
On systems that do not define `intmax_t`, we define our own variant like this:

https://github.com/openssl/openssl/blob/52e6c77ebc25590ac894ce67d83a02da07c6f01f/include/openssl/types.h#L236-L245

On 32-bit systems, `long` will typically be 32 bits, but `double` is often twice as large (64 bits).

This has an impact on `test/params_conversion_test.c` among others with the following stanza:

https://github.com/openssl/openssl/blob/52e6c77ebc25590ac894ce67d83a02da07c6f01f/test/recipes/04-test_params_conversion_data/native_types.txt#L76-L82

With these data, the following test fails:

https://github.com/openssl/openssl/blob/52e6c77ebc25590ac894ce67d83a02da07c6f01f/test/params_conversion_test.c#L288

This is due to this check in `OSSL_PARAM_set_double()`

https://github.com/openssl/openssl/blob/52e6c77ebc25590ac894ce67d83a02da07c6f01f/crypto/params.c#L1038

What's happening here, because `intmax_t` is 32 bits, is that the result of `(ossl_intmax_t)val` becaomes -2147483648, not 2147483648 (because that's how small ints work), and since `val` is the *double* 2147483648.0, they turn out not to be equal and `OSSL_PARAM_set_double()` fails.

review_comments:
Removing this loses the test for the value being integral.

I.e. val = 3.2 will convert to integer (3 or 4 depending on rounding mode) without error.
Hmmmm....  this will work but I'm not sure its the best way to go when converting real -> uint.  This approach is fine for converting uint -> real safely.
The more I think about this, the wronger it seems.
